No one can answer this question for you directly, especially not without more context. 

However, here are some things to consider:
1/ Your career is a marathon, not a sprint. Careers can take winding paths, they won't necessarily be straight lines up and to the right, and that is A-okay. It greatly depends on what you're trying to optimize in your life. Personally, I want to get paid AND enjoy my work.

2/ Given 1/, whether you choose PM or TPM should focus on what you want to prioritize. I would shift to the long game and think about the work most tied to each discipline. Do you want to have a bias on figuring out the market strategy and user experience? Then PM is likely the discipline you should think about. Do you want to stay really tied to the execution and the technical architecture? Then TPM might be the discipline you focus on. 

2a/ That said, PM and TPM are both very nebulous roles with a healthy amount of overlap. I've been both in my career, and I comfortably swap between my PM and TPM hats as needed depending on the program, problems, and personnel of any given situation.

2b/ Repeating again that career is a marathon, it is A-okay to switch between PM and TPM roles depending on the stage of your career. Do what makes sense for that given moment in your career, although you may have temporary downlevels on each swap.

3/ There is market data that several of the big companies everyone is gunning for will pay more for an equally leveled Product Manager compared to a Technical Program Manager. Is that fair? Who knows, capitalism means that your value is simply what you're able to convince someone to pay you. If you're optimizing literally 100% for compensation, this is worth considering.

3a/ As with everything, there is a caveat. This is for equally leveled PM vs TPM. If your current skillset and natural disposition mean you would top out at Principal TPM vs Senior PM, then maybe TPm is a better role to optimize for compensation. Again, this depends.

Does anyone have experience with helping a team develop their charter, mission, vision and annual roadmap ? A senior exec asked for my help with this. They are extremely frustrated with this particular team and its inability to articulate succinctly what their mission, vision , initiatives they will be working on and what kind of support/engagement they need from cross functional teams. I do not have prior experience with this so looking for help or pointers.

@noobTPM Writing a charter is like writing anything else: there isn't really a one-size-fits-all solution. You'll have to adapt to your team, your org, your tech stack, your team dynamics and politics 

That said, where I would start is by doing a listening tour with the team lead, a couple ICs, a couple peer team leads, and the executive chain. (Probably 1:1 conversations to start to get people's candid opinion). I said listening tour, not talking tour because your job is to focus on what others are saying and thinking so that you can synthesize that into a comprehensive, congruent, and crisp statement.

Some example questions I would ask:
How does the domain the team develops contribute to the org 's mission, vision, annual roadmap? (Ideally, how does the team directly impact specific business KPIs like revenue, cost, usage?)

What features/programs are the team currently working on toward above (cost and specific business impact per item)?

What features/programs have partners and stakeholders asked the team to develop (again, cost and specific business impact)?

What work would make the team itself develop more efficient/effective, e.g. runbooks, automation, documentation? (You guessed it, cost and specific business impact)

What tech debt does the team have that we need to account for? e.g. software/hardware hitting End of Life, new frameworks or technologies that we need to migrate to, migrations out of a monolith, etc. (do I need to say it again? Cost and specific business impact)

Something along the lines of "If you got 20% more headcount to do something right now, what would you spend it on?"

The tricky thing you'll have to navigate on your own is that your team likely has a ton of different work and ideas. As my name implies, your job is to find the highest *leverage* work the team should pursue. You might employ a framework like Weighted Shortest Job First, but this is gonna be a bit of art rather than science because your inputs are rarely truly objective metrics.

You may need to remind the team that we don't write code for fun at work. We write code to have a specific business impact. They may be distraught because they hear this and think it means they can't fund internal work important to their team's quality of life. Not true! Developer productivity is a very valid business impact. (e.g. refactoring truly bad spaghetti code that slows deploys and causes release bugs) But you'll have to work harder to prove that compared to "implementing this reduces our AWS bill by $X"
This is gold. Thanks @LeverageCoach Would the line of thinking /questions change if the team is not a developer team but rather a cybersecurity team ?

* How are we set up (or doing) currently and what are the challenges to get us to end state?

Happy to help. The overall direction of questions is the same, but you'll need to adapt as I mentioned above. Things to consider:

Your team is meant to enable partner teams, but this likely also means blocking them or slowing them down somehow). What do those partners have to say about that? (Be ready for harsh negative feedback, but see it as an opportunity)

Security is tricky to quantify business impact for because it's a literal arms race that you could spend infinite resources on getting "just a little bit more secure". So your questions around business impact will really need to be expected values: what is the probability of this security vulnerability biting us multiplied by the magnitude of the impact? 

e.g. implementing better authentication in the most external API layer is high value because it's hit by 95% of any malicious actors doing basic probes. But maybe implementing better security (e.g. encryption at rest) on the internal database of customer personal information is more important because even if it's not as likely that an attacker gets to the internal DB, the magnitude of pain your business goes through in the unlikely event is really high.

Looking for inputs. Our company has annual engineering offsites where topics include sharing the teams work, see some know how sessions, brainstorming on an architecture improvement or change. Any inputs on topics that TPMs can present in such form. We are invited and mostly listen in and more of background facilitators. Looking for ideas on topics a TPgm can present

1/ Consider their lack of ability to write things down as an ability to "influence without authority" using the "power of the pen". Write down your first rough draft, share it with the team with the caveat of "This is my understanding based on what you've told me, how can we improve this to better align with what believe?"

2/ Regarding approaching partner teams: I'm going to assume that your cybersecurity team is in charge of ensuring that the products your company releases are secure. What this usually means in practice is that product feature teams look at the cybersecurity team as "just another piece of red tape to get what I really want, a feature release". 

The best cybersecurity teams I've worked with are great partners that understand that security's role is not to be strict gatekeepers. Rather, the best partners get involved early to avoid last-minute surprise work and are flexible when it comes to what is and is not "allowed". I've had security engineers tell me "Hey, so I understand you've got a tight deadline to launch from execs, so it's okay for you to launch with these open issues as long as you get sign off from your VP and you have a plan to resolve within 30/60/90 days". 

So to figure out whether your cybersecurity team is doing well, you'll want to approach your partners and see whether security is seen as a partner or a gatekeeper. The framework I'd go with in your listening tour with partners is : "We're looking to be an effective partner that both balances the security needs of the company and your needs to launch products. Can we chat about 'What Went Well' vs. things we should "Take A Look At' ?" (WWW vs. TALA intentionally phrased)
@Borderline88 In this layoff-heavy environment, I would really, really caution against joking about entire organizations getting cut tomorrow. People are very sensitive to this right now.

@Legoblocks That's a fun challenge, but it's hard to prescribe something to present to a broad audience without more context. TPM is such a nebulous role and it's hard to tell what your TPM role focuses on at your company vs. what other companies do. Does your TPM discipline focus more heavily on planning and process? On driving deep technical issues? On communication and documentation channels? That's probably what you would want to present on. 

That said, here are some topics I've seen work well in a broad engineering offsite:
1/ "What do TPMs here do, and how can we help you be more effective? (I like "Help me, help you" as the call to action in this kind of presentation)

1a/ "When do you really need a TPM?" (Because no, our job isn't to schedule every meeting or file every Jira)

2/ "What's our prioritization process and how can you get what you care about funded?" (Again, focus on how TPMs can help the audience with their goals)

3/ One thing that I haven't done yet is a presentation on behavioral change based on Atomic Habits. The tentative title I have is "Reduce INCs, save money, and lose weight by ignoring goals". The thesis from Atomic Habits is that everybody and their mother knows how to set goals now, but few people achieve them. What really matters is understanding the cycle of Cue -> Craving -> Response -> Reward, and *setting up a system* to get the results you want. 

For example, if your team has a lot of INCs, it's kinda useless to set a goal of "We want fewer INCs" if there's no underlying implementation plan and system to achieve that. What are the various cues and responses the team needs to take set up to reduce INCs? 

Analogously: Most folks start the new year saying "I want to lose weight". But what tangible cues and responses are you using to get there? A simple cue-> response might be "Any time I reach for a drink, I will make sure it is water instead of soda". Enforce that by removing soda from your household.

The harsher the environment, the more people should do this exercise so the leaders can advertise the benefit of having the team. If their leaders don’t know the downside of cutting the team, they won’t hesitate when there’s pressure for headcount reduction.

I suspect you and I just have very different approaches. I agree it's prudent to advertise the business impact of the team. I disagree in that I think you can get that benefit of that without the con of broadly stating "pretend your team got laid off." I may be overly conservative here, but it's up to each person how they drive that conversation.

I am first TPM hire at my company and the entire company is working on setting goals for the year. Looking for guidance here on some ideas on what some goals and key results could be in my scenario where there has been no TPM role and the role is not entirely defined.
@noobTPM You want goals for you as an IC specifically? Or the broader team you're part of?
IC specifically

As you've probably noticed by my previous replies, I find it hard to provide specific guidance without more context.

That said, here's some stuff I would think about.
* What is the company struggling with the most that would be high-leverage for a TPM to make better? ( Portfolio planning? Cross-team execution? Single-team but high-value execution? Alignment on status and reporting? Alignment on technical strategy? Specific domains or programs?)
* Similarly, what is your manager & skip-level struggling with the most that would be high-leverage for a TPM to make better? (Sometimes this is the same as above, sometimes not)

* As a first TPM, you're likely responsible for setting the standard of what TPMs should and shouldn't do. Do you have a clear roles & responsibilities doc for what the discipline does? Does it include some form of RACI between TPM, PM, EM, QA, etc.? Are you responsible for hiring more TPMs, and what might goals there look like?

* As a first TPM, you're probably driving at least one or two high-value programs directly. I'd figure out a good set of program-specific goals there. (e.g. define and drive monolith split into microservices, define and drive cost reduction program, etc.)

* As a first TPM, you can't be everywhere at once. What are ways that you can influence the broader organization to run more smoothly even if you're not directly providing that lift? (Examples might be processes or automation you can set up)

Probably the most common gating factor in getting from manager to director is "Does this business org require a director of TPM to justify a promotion?"

Depending on how your organization interprets the title, Director typically implies at least a manager of managers. At minimum, assume 2 managers with 4 direct reports each, so that's 10 TPM HC underneath a Director. As organizations tighten HC, those are actually low ratios, so probably more like 15+ HC under a Director. Does your organization have enough justification for that many TPMs above you? Once that's settled, then you need to likely prove you can manage managers.

What do you do if there isn't business justification for promo? Well, you have to weigh leaving to find a role that does have business justification for promo. (This is true for all promos).

(For transparency, I benefited from some title inflation at my previous org. We had several first-level managers that were called Directors. My experience for TPMing ~10 years at Intel: working with silicon is tends to dictate rigid, waterfall like program structure: plan -> design -> pre-si -> tapeout -> post-si -> design -> tapeout steppings ... The schedule is defined by fab availability and manufacturing timelines (e.g. base layer 16wks, metal fixes 6wks) and everything flows from there. This is generally pretty different from how software companies do it.

My experience is that program managers have much tighter control and a more well defined charter of work. As a program manager at Intel, I could make decisions on schedule, design, bugs, quality, marketing, gtm and more. Intel is a top-down company so this may be somewhat different in NVidia for example thoughj I suspect not by much
Architects dealt with adding features to the silicon (often without market need but that's another story) while EMs owned the resources working in a given space.

Being a top-down company, EMs are required to understand and control what's going on in their space though this varied widely based on how technical they were. Some would be very technical and serve as the one stop shop for everything and others less so and we had to pull tech leads into the picture instead. Example can be a silicon bug is found weeks before tapeout and we need to make a decision whether to fix, how to fix and how it impacts the schedule. We could pull post-si validation and design directors/VPs to the discussion or we could work directly with the engineers working on the issue depending on the people.

sGiven what I know about your background, SV, I would expect some more structured thinking/response. 
I expect very senior TPMs to have multiple frameworks to approach problems, shaped by their experiences. I also expect them to have done research on how the particular company operates (tops-down/bottoms-up, consensus/committee based decisioning vs 1-person decider, functional org structures vs GM based models, etc.). And I expect the response to be more nuanced than the generic answer you've provided. 

To nitpick further : 
1/ Exec comms : 
  a/ clearly frame what type of forum it is : inform/escalate/product-review/data&priorites execution review/.. 
  b/ you should also talk about the format : async/live , slides/long-form-docs, data-heavy/UX & journeys, etc/ 
  c/ talk about frequency; if this is a recurring forum, you should def have a "what has happened so far" section 
  d/ if this is a multi-disciplinary forum, what does each VP care about ?
  e/ i know you talked about decisions; IMO, it is different from "what do we need from you" - which should also be something you call out. 

2/ Teams with diff priorities : i see some more structured/framework based response here; but then the assumption (teams probably prioritizing for diff goals) is decent, but probably something i expect from a mid-level TPM. 
  a/ is it a function of how the orgs are setup? is it by design? is it necessary to resolve the priority difference? is there appetite? 
  b/ is there a dependency between teams? 
  c/ how do u understand at what level the misalignment is ? and then how do u work to resolve at the diff levels?
